claim: Monomorium pharaonis workers show age-based division of labor between nurses and foragers.
source: We tracked cohorts of age-marked workers and recorded their behavior and location inside and outside the nest. In order to identify differentially expressed genes associated with age-based division of labor, we collected age-marked workers and workers observed performing specific behaviors. The observed location of workers from different age classes changed with both nest location and behavior (glm with quasipoisson errors and log link, both p < 0.01) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations and statistical analysis showing significant changes in worker location and behavior with age.

claim: The average age of workers observed nursing was 6.94 days.
source: Nursing and foraging were at the two extremes: the average age of workers observed nursing was 6.94 days and the average age of workers observed foraging (i.e., in the act of collecting food) was 13.04 days.
evidence: Directly measured from behavioral observations of age-marked workers.

claim: The average age of workers observed foraging was 13.04 days.
source: Nursing and foraging were at the two extremes: the average age of workers observed nursing was 6.94 days and the average age of workers observed foraging (i.e., in the act of collecting food) was 13.04 days.
evidence: Directly measured from behavioral observations of age-marked workers.

claim: There is a marked transition from nursing to foraging between 9 and 12 days of age in M. pharaonis workers.
source: There appeared to be a marked transition from nursing to foraging between 9 and 12 days of age (Figure 1A), with 75% of nursing observations made for workers less than 10 days old and 75% of foraging observations made for workers over 10 days old (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing the distribution of nursing and foraging observations across age classes.

claim: The M. pharaonis genome assembly is 284 mb with an N50 of 19.0 kb.
source: We chose k = 69 as a compromise between these two metrics, resulting in a scaffolded assembly of 284 mb, with a N50 of 19.0 kb.
evidence: Direct result from genome assembly analysis.

claim: CEGMA analysis found complete sequences for 92% of ultra-conserved eukaryotic genes in the M. pharaonis genome assembly.
source: CEGMA analysis (Parra et al., 2009) found complete sequences for 92% of the ultra-conserved eukaryotic genes, and partial sequences for 97%.
evidence: Result from CEGMA analysis of the genome assembly.

claim: Cufflinks assembly identified 22,385 transcribed loci in M. pharaonis.
source: Cufflinks assembly identified 22,385 transcribed loci.
evidence: Direct result from transcriptome assembly.

claim: There were 1217 forager-upregulated transcripts in M. pharaonis.
source: There were 1217 forager-upregulated, 1247 nurse-upregulated transcripts, and 14,907 transcripts that were not differentially expressed.
evidence: Result from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: There were 1247 nurse-upregulated transcripts in M. pharaonis.
source: There were 1217 forager-upregulated, 1247 nurse-upregulated transcripts, and 14,907 transcripts that were not differentially expressed.
evidence: Result from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: There were 14,907 transcripts that were not differentially expressed between nurses and foragers.
source: There were 1217 forager-upregulated, 1247 nurse-upregulated transcripts, and 14,907 transcripts that were not differentially expressed.
evidence: Result from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Gene expression patterns mirrored the behavioral transition from nursing to foraging around day 10.
source: Qualitatively, gene expression patterns mirrored the behavioral transition from nursing to foraging that we observed around day 10 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression data with behavioral observations.

claim: K-nearest neighbor classifier separated workers into two distinct classes based on age, assigning those younger than 12 days into the nurse class and the rest into the forager class.
source: After the KNN was trained on nurse and forager profiles, it clearly separated workers into two distinct classes based on age, assigning those younger than 12 days into the nurse class, and the rest into the forager class (Supplementary file 2 pages 14–15), suggesting a fairly discrete transcriptomic transition between the two behaviors.
evidence: Result from supervised learning analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes have a higher proportion of identified fire ant orthologs (0.54) compared to nurse-upregulated (0.43) and non-differentially expressed genes (0.43).
source: The proportion of genes with identified orthologs in the fire ant Solenopsis invicta differed between behavioral categories (Manfredini et al., 2014), with forager-upregulated genes having a higher proportion (0.54) relative to nurse-upregulated (0.43) and non-differentially expressed (0.43) (multiple comparison Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison of ortholog identification rates across gene categories.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes have a higher proportion of identified honey bee orthologs (0.50) compared to nurse-upregulated (0.38) and non-differentially expressed genes (0.38).
source: Similarly, the proportion of genes with identified honey bee A. mellifera orthologs was higher for forager-upregulated genes (0.50), relative to nurse-upregulated (0.38), and non-differentially expressed genes (0.38) (multiple comparison Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05) (note we used a less conservative BLAST threshold for the honey bee so that the proportions of honey bee and fire ant orthologs are not directly comparable, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Statistical comparison of ortholog identification rates across gene categories.

claim: Approximately half of non-differentially expressed (0.51) and nurse-upregulated (0.50) genes did not have orthologs identified in either the fire ant or honey bee genomes.
source: Furthermore, approximately half of non-differentially expressed (0.51) and nurse-upregulated (0.50) genes did not have orthologs identified in either the fire ant or honey bee genomes, but this proportion was lower for forager-upregulated genes (0.39)
evidence: Analysis of ortholog identification across two species.

claim: The proportion of forager-upregulated genes without orthologs in either fire ant or honey bee (0.39) is lower than for nurse-upregulated and non-differentially expressed genes.
source: Furthermore, approximately half of non-differentially expressed (0.51) and nurse-upregulated (0.50) genes did not have orthologs identified in either the fire ant or honey bee genomes, but this proportion was lower for forager-upregulated genes (0.39)
evidence: Analysis of ortholog identification across two species.

claim: The proportion of forager-upregulated genes with orthologs identified from both fire ants and honey bees (0.43) is higher compared to nurse-upregulated and non-differentially expressed genes (0.32).
source: correspondingly, the proportion of forager-upregulated genes with orthologs identified from both fire ants and honey bees was higher (0.43) compared to nurse-upregulated and non-differentially expressed genes (0.32) (X2 = 71.42, df = 6, p < 10−13).
evidence: Statistical analysis of ortholog identification patterns.

claim: Genes previously detected as upregulated in nurses of S. invicta were more likely to have identified M. pharaonis orthologs up-regulated in nurses (p = 0.0022).
source: Genes previously detected as upregulated in nurses and foragers of S. invicta were more likely to have identified M. pharaonis orthologs up-regulated in these contexts as well (p = 0.0022 and p = 0.040, respectively).
evidence: Statistical comparison of gene expression patterns between species.

claim: Genes previously detected as upregulated in foragers of S. invicta were more likely to have identified M. pharaonis orthologs up-regulated in foragers (p = 0.040).
source: Genes previously detected as upregulated in nurses and foragers of S. invicta were more likely to have identified M. pharaonis orthologs up-regulated in these contexts as well (p = 0.0022 and p = 0.040, respectively).
evidence: Statistical comparison of gene expression patterns between species.

claim: Only 3.8% (47/1247) of nurse genes were differentially expressed in the same context in both M. pharaonis and S. invicta.
source: However, the actual percentage of genes differentially expressed in the same context in these two ant data sets was small: 3.8% (47/1247) of nurse genes and 3.2% (39/1217) of forager genes
evidence: Direct comparison of differentially expressed gene lists between species.

claim: Only 3.2% (39/1217) of forager genes were differentially expressed in the same context in both M. pharaonis and S. invicta.
source: However, the actual percentage of genes differentially expressed in the same context in these two ant data sets was small: 3.8% (47/1247) of nurse genes and 3.2% (39/1217) of forager genes
evidence: Direct comparison of differentially expressed gene lists between species.

claim: There was a significant correlation (Spearman's rho = 0.14) in the change of expression for nurse and forager samples between S. invicta and M. pharaonis, explaining only 2% of the variance.
source: There was a significant correlation in the change of expression for nurse and forager samples, but one that explained only 2% of the variance (Spearman's rho = 0.14, 6324 genes, p < 10−16).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of genome-wide expression profiles between species.

claim: Previously identified forager-upregulated honey bee genes were not more likely to have M. pharaonis orthologs expressed in the same context (p = 0.99).
source: In contrast to the fire ant and pharaoh ant comparison, previously identified forager- and nurse-upregulated honey bee A. mellifera genes (Alaux et al., 2009) were not more likely to have M. pharaonis orthologs expressed in the same context (p = 0.99, p = 0.98, respectively), consistent with a previous comparison between S. invicta and A. mellifera (Manfredini et al., 2014).
evidence: Statistical comparison with previously published honey bee data.

claim: Previously identified nurse-upregulated honey bee genes were not more likely to have M. pharaonis orthologs expressed in the same context (p = 0.98).
source: In contrast to the fire ant and pharaoh ant comparison, previously identified forager- and nurse-upregulated honey bee A. mellifera genes (Alaux et al., 2009) were not more likely to have M. pharaonis orthologs expressed in the same context (p = 0.99, p = 0.98, respectively), consistent with a previous comparison between S. invicta and A. mellifera (Manfredini et al., 2014).
evidence: Statistical comparison with previously published honey bee data.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes were strongly enriched for nearly 50 metabolism-related GO terms with p < 10−5.
source: Nurse-upregulated genes were strongly enriched for a range of GO terms associated with metabolism (nearly 50 metabolism-related terms with p < 10−5; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of nurse-upregulated genes.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes were enriched for GO terms associated with signal transduction and gland morphogenesis.
source: Forager-upregulated genes had a more diffuse signal, being relatively more weakly enriched for various GO terms, for example, associated with signal transduction and gland morphogenesis.
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of forager-upregulated genes.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes showed underrepresented GO terms associated with metabolic processes and chromatin modification.
source: Forager-upregulated genes showed a more consistent signal for underrepresented terms, for example, GO terms associated with metabolic processes and chromatin modification (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of forager-upregulated genes.

claim: WGCNA identified 14 co-expression modules ranging in size from 83 to 4218 genes.
source: These settings resulted in 14 co-expression modules, ranging in size from 83 to 4218 genes (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Result from weighted gene co-expression network analysis.

claim: Module 1 eigengene was strongly negatively correlated with worker age (r = −0.95, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0038).
source: Eigengenes in two of the modules—1 and 14, which contained the most nurse and forager genes, respectively—were strongly correlated with worker age, although in opposite directions, suggesting their role in aging and age-based division of labor (r = −0.95, r = 0.91 and with FDR-adjusted p-values 0.0038, 0.023, respectively) (Supplementary file 2, page 24).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between module eigengenes and worker age.

claim: Module 14 eigengene was strongly positively correlated with worker age (r = 0.91, FDR-adjusted p = 0.023).
source: Eigengenes in two of the modules—1 and 14, which contained the most nurse and forager genes, respectively—were strongly correlated with worker age, although in opposite directions, suggesting their role in aging and age-based division of labor (r = −0.95, r = 0.91 and with FDR-adjusted p-values 0.0038, 0.023, respectively) (Supplementary file 2, page 24).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between module eigengenes and worker age.

claim: Most module eigengenes switched signs during the period between 9 and 12 days, corresponding to the behavioral transition from nursing to foraging.
source: Interestingly, most module eigengenes switched signs during the period between 9 and 12 days, corresponding to the behavioral transition from nursing to foraging.
evidence: Analysis of module eigengene expression patterns across worker age.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes were concentrated in just a few modules, with only two modules containing more than 100 forager-upregulated genes.
source: Forager-upregulated genes were concentrated in just a few modules, with only two modules containing more than 100 forager-upregulated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Analysis of the distribution of forager-upregulated genes across modules.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes were more widely distributed, with five modules having more than 100 nurse-upregulated genes.
source: In contrast, nurse-upregulated genes were more widely distributed, with five modules having more than 100 nurse-upregulated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Analysis of the distribution of nurse-upregulated genes across modules.

claim: Module 5, which contained 116 nurse-upregulated genes, was enriched for terms associated with female gonad development.
source: Module 5, which contained 116 nurse-upregulated genes, was also enriched for terms associated with female gonad development, which is surprising given that M. pharaonis workers lack ovaries and are completely sterile.
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of module 5.

claim: M. pharaonis workers lack ovaries and are completely sterile.
source: Module 5, which contained 116 nurse-upregulated genes, was also enriched for terms associated with female gonad development, which is surprising given that M. pharaonis workers lack ovaries and are completely sterile.
evidence: Statement of biological fact about M. pharaonis workers.

claim: The proportion of module genes with identified S. invicta orthologs ranged from 0.28 to 0.53.
source: The proportion of module genes with identified S. invicta orthologs ranged from 0.28 to 0.53 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that in addition to being involved in different functions, the modules are composed of different proportions of conserved and taxonomically restricted genes.
evidence: Analysis of ortholog identification rates across modules.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes were much more connected than nurse or non-differentially expressed genes.
source: Forager-upregulated genes were much more connected than nurse or non-differentially expressed genes, while nurse-upregulated genes were less connected than non-differentially expressed genes (Figure 2A) (multiple comparison Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison of network connectivity across gene categories.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes were less connected than non-differentially expressed genes.
source: Forager-upregulated genes were much more connected than nurse or non-differentially expressed genes, while nurse-upregulated genes were less connected than non-differentially expressed genes (Figure 2A) (multiple comparison Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison of network connectivity across gene categories.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes evolve more rapidly than non-differentially expressed genes.
source: There was a small but significant difference in evolutionary rate dN/dS (Figure 2C), with nurse-upregulated genes evolving more rapidly than non-differentially expressed genes (multiple comparison Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison of evolutionary rates across gene categories.

claim: Nurse and forager genes were more highly expressed than non-differentially expressed genes.
source: Nurse and forager genes were also more highly expressed (Figure 2B) than non-differentially expressed genes (Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.05), although this last comparison is likely biased because differential expression is more easily detected in highly expressed genes.
evidence: Statistical comparison of expression levels across gene categories, with acknowledgment of potential bias.

claim: Co-expression network connectivity is negatively associated with evolutionary rate (r = −0.15, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: Co-expression network connectivity and expression level were overall negatively associated with evolutionary rate, such that highly connected and highly expressed genes had decreased rates of molecular evolution (Figure 2D,E; evolutionary rate and connectivity, r = −0.15, p < 2 × 10−16; evolutionary rate and expression, measured in terms of transcriptional abundance, fragments per million reads mapped, FPKM, r = −0.12, p < 2 × 10−16)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between connectivity and evolutionary rate.

claim: Expression level is negatively associated with evolutionary rate (r = −0.12, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: Co-expression network connectivity and expression level were overall negatively associated with evolutionary rate, such that highly connected and highly expressed genes had decreased rates of molecular evolution (Figure 2D,E; evolutionary rate and connectivity, r = −0.15, p < 2 × 10−16; evolutionary rate and expression, measured in terms of transcriptional abundance, fragments per million reads mapped, FPKM, r = −0.12, p < 2 × 10−16)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between expression and evolutionary rate.

claim: Connectivity and expression are positively correlated (r = 0.30, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: and connectivity and expression were positively correlated (r = 0.30, p < 2 × 10−16).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between connectivity and expression.

claim: In a full model of evolutionary rate, the largest effects were main effects of expression (z = −7.42, p = 1.29 × 10−13) and connectivity (z = −3.69, p = 0.00023).
source: In a full model considering how a gene's rate of molecular evolution depended on its gene expression level, network connectedness, and behavioral category, the largest effects were main effects of expression (z = −7.42, p = 1.29 × 10−13) and connectivity (z = −3.69, p = 0.00023).
evidence: Statistical modeling of factors affecting evolutionary rate.

claim: Genes with orthologs in the fire ant or honey bee had greater connectivity and expression.
source: Overall, genes with orthologs in the fire ant or honey bee had greater connectivity and expression (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of connectivity and expression between genes with and without identified orthologs.

claim: Connectivity had the strongest effect on whether a gene had an S. invicta ortholog (t = 24.5, p < 10−16).
source: In considering a model with both main and interaction effects of behavioral category, expression level, and connectivity, connectivity had the strongest effect (glm with quasibinomial residuals: t = 24.5, p < 10−16, for the presence of S. invicta orthologs; t = 32.2, p < 10−16, for the presence of A. mellifera orthologs), with more highly connected genes being more likely to have an ortholog.
evidence: Statistical modeling of factors affecting ortholog identification.

claim: Connectivity had the strongest effect on whether a gene had an A. mellifera ortholog (t = 32.2, p < 10−16).
source: In considering a model with both main and interaction effects of behavioral category, expression level, and connectivity, connectivity had the strongest effect (glm with quasibinomial residuals: t = 24.5, p < 10−16, for the presence of S. invicta orthologs; t = 32.2, p < 10−16, for the presence of A. mellifera orthologs), with more highly connected genes being more likely to have an ortholog.
evidence: Statistical modeling of factors affecting ortholog identification.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes had fewer S. invicta orthologs than expected given their connectivities (t = −3.17, p = 0.0015).
source: There were also much smaller interaction effects indicating that nurse-upregulated genes had fewer orthologs than expected given their connectivities (i.e., connectivity had a weaker effect on nurse-upregulated genes than other genes, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; t = −3.17, p = 0.0015 for S. invicta orthologs; t = −2.76, p = 0.0057 for A. mellifera orthologs)
evidence: Statistical modeling showing interaction effects between gene category and connectivity.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes had fewer A. mellifera orthologs than expected given their connectivities (t = −2.76, p = 0.0057).
source: There were also much smaller interaction effects indicating that nurse-upregulated genes had fewer orthologs than expected given their connectivities (i.e., connectivity had a weaker effect on nurse-upregulated genes than other genes, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; t = −3.17, p = 0.0015 for S. invicta orthologs; t = −2.76, p = 0.0057 for A. mellifera orthologs)
evidence: Statistical modeling showing interaction effects between gene category and connectivity.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes had fewer S. invicta orthologs than expected given their expression (t = −2.33, p = 0.02).
source: and forager-upregulated genes had fewer orthologs than expected given their expression (t = −2.33, p = 0.02 for S. invicta orthologs; t = −2.58, p = 0.0098 for A. mellifera orthologs; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical modeling showing interaction effects between gene category and expression.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes had fewer A. mellifera orthologs than expected given their expression (t = −2.58, p = 0.0098).
source: and forager-upregulated genes had fewer orthologs than expected given their expression (t = −2.33, p = 0.02 for S. invicta orthologs; t = −2.58, p = 0.0098 for A. mellifera orthologs; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical modeling showing interaction effects between gene category and expression.

claim: Pharaoh ant and fire ant diverged on the order of 50 million years ago.
source: Such low overlap seems surprising, given that these two ants are in closely related ant genera, having diverged on the order of 50 Mya (Ward et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from phylogenetic study.

claim: Honey bees and ants diverged approximately 170 million years ago.
source: While we expected decreased overlap given that honey bees and ants diverged longer ago, ∼170 Mya (Ronquist et al., 2012), and represent independent origins of eusociality
evidence: Cited from phylogenetic study.

claim: Honey bees and ants represent independent origins of eusociality.
source: While we expected decreased overlap given that honey bees and ants diverged longer ago, ∼170 Mya (Ronquist et al., 2012), and represent independent origins of eusociality
evidence: Cited phylogenetic and evolutionary information.

claim: The genetic toolkit hypothesis proposes that a conserved set of genes and gene pathways involved in core physiological processes has been repeatedly used in the evolution of complex social behavior.
source: The genetic toolkit hypothesis and related hypotheses propose that a conserved set of genes and gene pathways involved in core physiological processes such as metabolism and reproduction has been repeatedly used in the evolution of complex social behavior in diverse lineages (West-Eberhard, 1996; Amdam et al., 2004, 2006; Toth and Robinson, 2007; Toth et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: The novel social genes hypothesis proposes that genes underlying social behavior are often novel socially acting genes or genes with novel social functions not present in solitary ancestors.
source: The novel social genes hypothesis proposes that genes underlying social behavior are often novel socially acting genes or are genes with novel social functions not present in solitary ancestors (Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010; Johnson and Tsutsui, 2011; Sumner, 2014).
evidence: Description of hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Highly conserved genes underpinning core physiological processes can also influence behavioral state.
source: The main conclusion of a decade of sociogenomic research with a range of solitary and social animal species is that highly conserved genes underpinning core physiological processes can also influence behavioral state (Amdam et al., 2004, 2006; Toth and Robinson, 2007; Toth et al., 2007, 2010; Woodard et al., 2011; Woodard et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The insulin signaling pathway, which mediates an organism's response to its internal nutritional state, also influences its behavior.
source: For example, the insulin signaling pathway, which mediates an organism's response to its internal nutritional state, also influences its behavior (Ament et al., 2008).
evidence: Example from cited study.

claim: The degree of a gene's connectivity to the rest of the regulatory network and its level of expression is often negatively correlated with its rate of molecular evolution.
source: Research in a range of model organisms demonstrates that the degree of a gene's connectivity to the rest of the regulatory network and its level of expression is often negatively correlated with its rate of molecular evolution (Krylov et al., 2003; Hahn and Kern, 2005; Jovelin and Phillips, 2009; Ramsay et al., 2009).
evidence: General principle from multiple cited studies.

claim: Highly connected 'hub' genes are often highly expressed and evolutionarily conserved.
source: For example, highly connected 'hub' genes are often highly expressed and evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: General principle from the literature, following from the previous cited statement.

claim: Genes associated with the expression of worker traits experience elevated rates of molecular evolution.
source: Previous research has compared rates of molecular evolution for genes associated with reproductive division of labor in social insects (Hunt et al., 2010, 2013; Harpur et al., 2014), as well as other conditionally expressed phenotypes in other organisms (Brisson and Nuzhdin, 2008; Leichty et al., 2012; Purandare et al., 2014), indicating that genes associated with the expression of worker traits experience elevated rates of molecular evolution.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Age polyethism involves the progression of workers from in-nest tasks such as nursing to outside-nest tasks such as foraging.
source: Age polyethism involves the progression of workers from in-nest tasks such as nursing to outside-nest tasks such as foraging.
evidence: Definition of age polyethism based on established knowledge.

claim: Age polyethism is a trait expressed by the functionally sterile worker caste and is expected to be shaped primarily through kin selection.
source: Because age polyethism is a trait expressed by the functionally sterile worker caste, it is expected to be shaped primarily through kin selection (Hamilton, 1964).
evidence: Theoretical expectation based on kin selection theory.

claim: The molecular underpinnings of age polyethism have only been well studied in the honey bee Apis mellifera.
source: While age polyethism plays a central role in the functioning of many eusocial systems (Hölldobler and Wilson, 2009), the molecular underpinnings have only been well studied in the honey bee Apis mellifera (Whitfield et al., 2006; Ament et al., 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2011), so that the genetic and evolutionary basis of age polyethism is not generally understood outside of honey bees.
evidence: Summary of the state of knowledge from cited literature.

claim: M. pharaonis workers are expected to live 9–10 weeks.
source: Previous literature indicates that M. pharaonis workers are expected to live 9–10 weeks (Peacock and Baxter, 1950), but our preliminary trials with our setup indicated that workers tend to die or lose their paint marks after several weeks.
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: Nestmate recognition is at most weak and transient in M. pharaonis.
source: Nestmate recognition is at most weak and transient in M. pharaonis (Schmidt et al., 2010), and callows in particular are readily accepted.
evidence: Cited from previous study.

claim: The genetic architecture of social behavior includes both highly connected and conserved components as well as loosely connected and evolutionarily labile components.
source: Our results indicate that the genetic architecture of social behavior includes both highly connected and conserved components as well as loosely connected and evolutionarily labile components.
evidence: Main conclusion synthesized from the study's findings.

claim: Forager-upregulated genes were much more highly connected and conserved, while nurse-upregulated genes were less connected and more evolutionarily labile.
source: However, compared to the rest of the genome, forager-upregulated genes were much more highly connected and conserved, while nurse-upregulated genes were less connected and more evolutionarily labile.
evidence: Summary of key findings from the study.

claim: Nurse- and forager-upregulated genes had distinct regulatory and evolutionary patterns relative to each other and to the rest of the transcriptome.
source: In addition to these genome-wide patterns, nurse- and forager-upregulated genes had distinct regulatory and evolutionary patterns relative to each other and to the rest of the transcriptome (Figures 2, 3).
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: Both conserved and novel genes likely play roles in the evolution of all new traits.
source: Furthermore, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, since both conserved and novel genes likely play roles in the evolution of all new traits (Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010; Woodard et al., 2011).
evidence: Synthesis of ideas from cited literature.

claim: All worker traits in Monomorium ants are expected to be shaped exclusively by indirect selection (kin selection) because workers are obligately sterile.
source: As Monomorium ant workers are obligately sterile, all worker traits are expected to be shaped exclusively by indirect selection (i.e., kin selection) (Hamilton, 1964).
evidence: Theoretical expectation based on kin selection theory and the biology of M. pharaonis.

claim: Indirect selection is weaker than direct selection, proportional to relatedness.
source: All-else-equal, such indirect selection is weaker than direct selection, proportional to relatedness (Hamilton, 1964), and a priori is expected to produce relaxed selective constraint and elevated rates of molecular evolution for all genes associated with worker traits (Linksvayer and Wade, 2009).
evidence: Theoretical principle from kin selection theory.

claim: Most studies have found that worker-biased genes are more rapidly evolving than queen-biased genes.
source: Past studies have found different rates of molecular evolution for worker-biased and queen-biased genes, with most studies finding that worker-biased genes are more rapidly evolving (Ferreira et al., 2013; Feldmeyer et al., 2014; Harpur et al., 2014; but see; Hunt et al., 2010).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Social evolution does not just have simple genome-wide effects but instead shapes complex social traits while acting within general systems-level constraints imposed by regulatory architecture.
source: These results suggest that social evolution does not just have simple genome-wide effects such as relaxed effective selection associated with kin selection, but instead shapes complex social traits while acting within general systems-level constraints imposed by regulatory architecture.
evidence: Interpretation and synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Genes influencing many key social traits are not only conditionally expressed, but are also located peripherally within regulatory networks, and so are relatively unconstrained.
source: The common perception that social evolution often involves rapid evolutionary dynamics (West-Eberhard, 1983; Tanaka, 1996; Moore et al., 1997; Wolf et al., 1999; Nonacs, 2011; Bailey and Moore, 2012; Van Dyken and Wade, 2012) may result from the fact that genes influencing many key social traits are not only conditionally expressed, but are also located peripherally within regulatory networks, and so are relatively unconstrained.
evidence: Interpretation combining cited literature with the study's findings.

claim: Traits associated with social signal production (e.g., pheromone and glandular secretions) are often located peripherally within regulatory networks and may be evolutionarily labile.
source: For example, we expect that traits associated with social signal production (e.g., pheromone and glandular secretions) are often located peripherally within regulatory networks and as a result may be evolutionarily labile (Jasper et al., 2015), as is the case more generally with secreted proteins (Julenius and Pedersen, 2006; Liao et al., 2010; Nogueira et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference based on cited literature about secreted proteins.

claim: Novel genes are likely added peripherally to regulatory networks during the evolution of social novelty.
source: These arguments suggest how both conserved, toolkit genes, as well as rapidly evolving and taxonomically restricted novel genes, likely play important roles in the evolution of social novelty, with novel genes being added peripherally to regulatory networks.
evidence: Synthesis and interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: M. pharaonis age-based division of labor has a complex genetic basis with some components that are highly connected and conserved, and other components that are more loosely connected and evolutionarily labile.
source: Our results are consistent with this interpretation, because M. pharaonis age-based division of labor seems to have a complex genetic basis with some components that are highly connected and conserved, and other components that are more loosely connected and evolutionarily labile.
evidence: Summary and interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Nurse-upregulated genes are more rapidly evolving and less conserved among social insect lineages relative to forager-upregulated genes.
source: Our findings that nurse-upregulated genes are more rapidly evolving and less conserved among social insect lineages relative to forager-upregulated genes suggest that nurse traits have been a major focus of evolutionary innovation between social insect lineages.
evidence: Summary of key findings from the study.

claim: Nurse traits have been a major focus of evolutionary innovation between social insect lineages.
source: Our findings that nurse-upregulated genes are more rapidly evolving and less conserved among social insect lineages relative to forager-upregulated genes suggest that nurse traits have been a major focus of evolutionary innovation between social insect lineages.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings about evolutionary rates and conservation.

claim: The physiological mechanisms associated with metabolically costly foraging activities and older adult life may be relatively conserved and simple.
source: One explanation is that the physiological mechanisms associated with metabolically costly foraging activities and older adult life (M. pharaonis workers usually only live several weeks [Peacock and Baxter, 1950], so that foragers which start right before their second week of age may already be senescing) may be relatively conserved and simple.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed patterns, citing worker lifespan.

claim: Nursing behavior may involve more diverse physiological and developmental processes than foraging.
source: Nursing behavior, occurring during very early adult life, may involve more diverse physiological and developmental processes, and nursing itself may also involve more diverse behaviors and physiological processes, such as food processing and the synthesis of glandular secretions that are fed to larvae.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed patterns.

claim: The relatively more complex genetic architecture of nursing has served as less of a constraint and facilitated more evolutionary change for nurse-related genes.
source: Perhaps the relatively more complex genetic architecture (less tightly connected, involving more modules, and diverse processes) has served as less of a constraint and facilitated more evolutionary change for nurse-related genes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Nurse-specific functions and functions for early adult life may be generally more evolutionarily labile as well as more physiologically and behaviorally labile within and across lineages than forager-specific functions.
source: If so, we predict that nurse-specific functions and functions for early adult life may be generally more evolutionarily labile as well as more physiologically and behaviorally labile within and across lineages than forager-specific functions.
evidence: Prediction based on the study's findings and interpretation.

claim: Obligate sterility may release workers from constraints on the evolution of genes acting early in worker development.
source: Note that this prediction is opposite the typical expectation that genes acting early in development have more pleiotropic effects and are thus especially constrained (Roux and Robinson-Rechavi, 2008; Piasecka et al., 2013), but obligate sterility may, in part, release workers from these constraints on the evolution of genes acting early in worker development.
evidence: Speculative explanation contrasting with typical developmental constraints, citing relevant literature.

claim: The majority of forager-upregulated genes were contained within a single gene module (module 14) that was significantly positively associated with age.
source: The majority of forager-upregulated genes were contained within a single gene module (module 14; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that was significantly positively associated with age.
evidence: Result from WGCNA analysis.

claim: Another module with expression negatively associated with age contained the largest number of nurse genes.
source: Another module with expression negatively associated with age contained the largest number of nurse genes, but nurse genes were also broadly spread out across a number of other modules with complex expression patterns across age and behavioral groups.
evidence: Result from WGCNA analysis.

claim: The modules differed in the proportion of constituent genes which had identifiable S. invicta and A. mellifera orthologs.
source: Interestingly, the modules differed in the proportion of constituent genes which had identifiable S. invicta and A. mellifera orthologs, indicating that modules vary in the degree to which they are composed of conserved genes and gene networks vs rapidly evolving genes with unknown function.
evidence: Analysis of ortholog identification rates across modules.

claim: Modules vary in the degree to which they are composed of conserved genes and gene networks vs rapidly evolving genes with unknown function.
source: Interestingly, the modules differed in the proportion of constituent genes which had identifiable S. invicta and A. mellifera orthologs, indicating that modules vary in the degree to which they are composed of conserved genes and gene networks vs rapidly evolving genes with unknown function.
evidence: Inference from the variation in ortholog identification rates across modules.

claim: Two replicate M. pharaonis observation colonies were established, each with 10 queens, approximately 4000 workers, and 1000 brood.
source: Two replicate M. pharaonis observation colonies were established, each with 10 queens, approximately 4000 workers, and 1000 brood, representing a random subsample of a larger source colony.
evidence: Description of experimental setup.

claim: Every 3 days, 600 newly eclosed callow workers were collected and paint marked with a unique age cohort color dot.
source: Every 3 days, 600 newly eclosed callow workers, which were inferred to be approximately 0–1 days old, were collected from 8–10 stock colonies. These callow workers were briefly anesthetized with CO2 and individually paint marked on the gaster with a unique age cohort color dot using a Sharpie extra fine oil based paint pen, and then 300 were added to each of the observation colonies.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Five uniquely marked age cohorts were added to the colonies on days 1, 4, 7, 10, and 13 of the study.
source: Five uniquely marked age cohorts were thus added to the colonies on days 1, 4, 7, 10, and 13 of the study.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The study was run for 1 month to capture the major age-based transitions in worker behavior.
source: We ran the study for 1 month, expecting to capture the major age-based transitions in worker behavior (e.g., the nursing to foraging transition observed in other species), but it is possible that we missed late behavioral transitions that occurred towards the end of workers' lives.
evidence: Description of study duration and rationale.

claim: A behavioral scan of each colony was completed once each day for the duration of the month-long study.
source: A behavioral scan of each colony was completed once each day for the duration of the month-long study by recording the instantaneous behavior and location observed for every visible paint-marked worker.
evidence: Description of data collection procedure.

claim: 30 distinct behaviors were recorded, but only 15 were observed more than 15 total times during the study period.
source: We recorded 30 distinct behaviors, but only 15 were observed more than 15 total times during the study period (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Summary of behavioral observations.

claim: Each experimental colony contained four identifiable locations: brood area, brood periphery, remaining nest area, and foraging area.
source: Each experimental colony contained four identifiable locations that were redefined prior to each behavioral scan: brood area, brood periphery, remaining nest area, and foraging area.
evidence: Description of spatial categories used in the study.

claim: Every 3 days, whole bodies of five individuals from each available uniquely paint marked age cohort were collected, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C.
source: Every 3 days, whole bodies of five individuals from each available uniquely paint marked age cohort were collected, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C.
evidence: Description of sample collection procedure.

claim: 20 individuals of each age category were pooled for whole body RNA extraction for each of the two replicate observation colonies.
source: This sampling scheme resulted in seven groups of individuals of known age (0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, and 18+ days old). 20 individuals of each of these age category were pooled for whole body RNA extraction for each of the two replicate observation colonies.
evidence: Description of RNA extraction sample preparation.

claim: In total there were 24 libraries: 2 colony replicates × (7 age groups + 5 behavioral groups).
source: In total there were 24 libraries: 2 colony replicates × (7 age groups + 5 behavioral groups).
evidence: Description of the total number of RNA-seq libraries.

claim: DNA from a single haploid male was used to prepare a TruSeq library for genome sequencing.
source: DNA from a single haploid male (183 ng) was used to prepare a TruSeq library, which was sequenced in multiplex on an Illumina HiSeq 2000, yielding 70,894,179 million 100 bp read pairs.
evidence: Description of genome sequencing procedure.

claim: Fire ant orthologs for each gene were determined using reciprocal best BLASTP with cutoffs of 10−10.
source: Fire ant (S. invicta) orthologs for each gene were determined using reciprocal best BLASTP, using cutoffs of 10−10.
evidence: Description of ortholog identification method.

claim: Pairwise dN/dS ratios for each gene were computed using the branch model in PAML (v. 4.6).
source: We then computed the pairwise dN/dS ratios for each gene using the branch model in PAML (v. 4.6).
evidence: Description of evolutionary rate calculation method.
